question: Where are the outside left and right side convex mirrors located on a school bus, and what do they help the driver monitor?
choice_a: Located below the outside flat mirrors; used to monitor the left and right sides of the bus at a wide angle, showing traffic, clearances, and students at the side of the bus
choice_b: Mounted on the front corners of the bus; used to see the danger zone directly in front of the bus
choice_c: Located above the outside flat mirrors; used only to check tire tread wear
choice_d: Mounted above the windshield; used to monitor passenger activity inside the bus
explanation: The convex mirrors are located below the outside flat mirrors and are used to monitor the left and right sides at a wide angle, providing a view of traffic, clearances, and students at the side of the bus.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 10 - School Buses, p. 10-1

question: What is the primary purpose of the outside left and right-side crossover mirrors mounted on the front corners of a school bus?
choice_a: To see the front bumper "danger zone" area directly in front of the bus that is not visible by direct vision, and the danger zone to the sides including the service door and front wheel area
choice_b: To see traffic in the lane at least one lane away on either side of the bus
choice_c: To check the front tires for proper inflation
choice_d: To monitor passenger activity inside the bus
explanation: The crossover mirrors are mounted on both front corners of the bus and are used to see the front bumper danger zone directly in front of the bus, as well as the danger zone to the left side and right side, including the service door and front wheel area.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 10 - School Buses, p. 10-2

question: According to the manual, how far behind the bus can the blind spot area beginning at the rear bumper extend when using the overhead inside rearview mirror?
choice_a: Up to 50 feet
choice_b: Up to 400 feet or more
choice_c: Up to 10 feet
choice_d: Up to 100 feet
explanation: The overhead inside rearview mirror has a large blind spot that begins at the rear bumper and could extend up to 400 feet or more behind the bus, requiring the driver to use exterior side mirrors to monitor that area.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 10 - School Buses, p. 10-2

question: Under what circumstance may a school bus driver change the location of an official school bus stop?
choice_a: At the driver's own discretion if traffic conditions warrant it
choice_b: Never, under any circumstances, once a route has been established
choice_c: With verbal permission from a parent at the stop
choice_d: Only with written approval from the appropriate school district official
explanation: The manual states a driver should never change the location of a bus stop without written approval from the appropriate school district official, meaning it can be changed only with that written approval.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 10 - School Buses, p. 10-2

question: If a school bus is equipped with alternating flashing amber warning lights, when should the driver activate them before the school bus stop?
choice_a: Only after coming to a complete stop
choice_b: At least 100 feet or approximately 3-5 seconds before the stop
choice_c: At least 200 feet or approximately 5-10 seconds before the stop, or in accordance with state law
choice_d: At least 500 feet or approximately 15-20 seconds before the stop
explanation: The driver should activate alternating flashing amber warning lights at least 200 feet or approximately 5-10 seconds before the school bus stop, or in accordance with state law.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 10 - School Buses, p. 10-2

question: When approaching a school bus stop, when should the driver turn on the right turn signal indicator?
choice_a: About 200 feet or approximately 5-10 seconds before pulling over
choice_b: About 500 feet or approximately 10-15 seconds before pulling over
choice_c: Only after the bus has come to a complete stop
choice_d: About 100-300 feet or approximately 3-5 seconds before pulling over
explanation: The right turn signal indicator should be turned on about 100-300 feet or approximately 3-5 seconds before pulling over.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 10 - School Buses, p. 10-2

question: When stopping to load students at a designated stop, how far away from the students should the front bumper of the school bus be, and why?
choice_a: As close as possible, so students do not have to walk far
choice_b: At least 10 feet away, which forces students to walk to the bus so the driver has a better view of their movements
choice_c: Exactly 5 feet away, so students can board quickly
choice_d: At least 20 feet away, to give the driver more room to angle the bus
explanation: The manual instructs bringing the bus to a full stop with the front bumper at least 10 feet away from students at the designated stop, which forces students to walk to the bus so the driver has a better view of their movements.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 10 - School Buses, p. 10-2

question: After unloading students along the route, how far should students be told to walk away from the side of the school bus?
choice_a: At least 25 feet, to fully clear the danger zone
choice_b: At least 5 feet, near the front bumper
choice_c: Students should remain directly beside the bus until the driver signals
choice_d: At least 10 feet, to a position where the driver can plainly see all students
explanation: During unloading on the route, students should be told to exit the bus and walk at least 10 feet away from the side of the bus to a position where the driver can plainly see all students.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 10 - School Buses, p. 10-3

question: When students must cross the roadway after exiting the bus, where should they walk to first, per the recommended procedure?
choice_a: To a location at least 10 feet in front of the right corner of the bumper, while remaining away from the front of the school bus
choice_b: To a location at least 10 feet behind the rear bumper
choice_c: To the middle of the roadway to signal oncoming traffic
choice_d: Directly across from the service door
explanation: Students crossing the roadway should walk approximately 10 feet away from the side of the bus to where the driver can see them, then to a location at least 10 feet in front of the right corner of the bumper, while remaining away from the front of the bus.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 10 - School Buses, p. 10-3

question: If a student drops an object near the bus during loading or unloading, what should the student be told to do?
choice_a: Leave the object and move to a point of safety out of the danger zones, then try to get the driver's attention to retrieve it
choice_b: Ask another student to retrieve the object
choice_c: Quickly pick it up and move to the bus door
choice_d: Wait next to the object until the bus departs
explanation: Students should be told to leave any dropped object and move to a point of safety out of the danger zones, and attempt to get the driver's attention to retrieve the object, since stopping to pick it up could cause the student to disappear from the driver's sight at a dangerous moment.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 10 - School Buses, p. 10-4

question: What safety hazard does the manual warn about regarding the handrail as students exit the bus?
choice_a: The handrail conducts electricity during electrical storms
choice_b: Clothing, accessories, or parts of a student's body can get caught in the handrail or door, causing injury or death
choice_c: The handrail can become slippery in wet weather, causing students to slip
choice_d: The handrail can obstruct the driver's view of exiting students
explanation: The manual warns that students have been injured or killed when clothing, accessories, or parts of their body get caught in the handrail or door as they exited the bus, so the driver should closely observe exiting students.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 10 - School Buses, p. 10-4

question: During a post-trip inspection of a school bus, what should the driver walk through the bus looking for?
choice_a: Articles left on the bus, sleeping students, open windows and doors, mechanical/operational problems, and damage or vandalism
choice_b: Only the presence of a first aid kit and fire extinguisher
choice_c: Only whether the emergency exits are locked
choice_d: Only fuel level and tire pressure
explanation: The post-trip inspection requires the driver to walk through and around the bus looking for articles left on the bus, sleeping students, open windows and doors, mechanical/operational problems, and damage or vandalism.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 10 - School Buses, p. 10-5

question: Per the manual's guidance on determining a safe place during a bus evacuation, how far off the road, in the direction of oncoming traffic, should a safe place generally be located?
choice_a: At least 50 feet
choice_b: At least 300 feet
choice_c: At least 25 feet
choice_d: At least 100 feet
explanation: A safe place will be at least 100 feet off the road in the direction of oncoming traffic, which helps keep students from being hit by debris if another vehicle collides with the bus.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 10 - School Buses, p. 10-6

question: If there is a risk from spilled hazardous materials during a bus evacuation, how far upwind of the bus should the driver lead students?
choice_a: At least 100 feet
choice_b: At least 50 feet
choice_c: At least 500 feet
choice_d: At least 300 feet
explanation: The manual instructs the driver to lead students upwind of the bus at least 300 feet if there is a risk from spilled hazardous materials.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 10 - School Buses, p. 10-6

question: According to the manual, which of the following requires a school bus driver to evacuate the bus?
choice_a: The bus air conditioning has stopped working
choice_b: A student reports feeling carsick
choice_c: The bus is running 15 minutes behind schedule
choice_d: The bus is on fire or there is a threat of a fire
explanation: The manual lists mandatory evacuation conditions, including when the bus is on fire or there is a threat of a fire, is stalled on or adjacent to a railroad-highway crossing, faces imminent danger of collision, or needs quick evacuation due to a hazardous materials spill.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 10 - School Buses, p. 10-5

question: What distinguishes a "passive" railroad-highway crossing from an "active" crossing?
choice_a: A passive crossing has flashing lights but no bells, while active crossings have both lights and bells
choice_b: A passive crossing only occurs on rural roads, while active crossings only occur in cities
choice_c: A passive crossing requires a police officer to be present at all times
choice_d: A passive crossing has no traffic control device, so the decision to proceed rests entirely with the driver; an active crossing has a traffic control device such as flashing red lights and/or gates
explanation: A passive crossing does not have any type of traffic control device, and the decision to proceed rests entirely in the driver's hands, while an active crossing has a traffic control device installed, such as flashing red lights with or without bells, or gates.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 10 - School Buses, p. 10-7

question: What is a driver required to do at a railroad crossing marked only with a cross-buck sign and no traffic signal?
choice_a: Yield the right-of-way to the train, and stop the bus before the cross-buck sign if there is no white line painted on the pavement
choice_b: Wait for a police officer to direct traffic before proceeding
choice_c: Only slow down, since cross-buck signs do not require a full stop
choice_d: Proceed without stopping if no train is visible
explanation: The cross-buck sign requires the driver to yield the right-of-way to the train, and if there is no white line painted on the pavement, the driver must stop the bus before the cross-buck sign.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 10 - School Buses, p. 10-7

question: At a railroad-highway crossing equipped with gates and flashing red lights, when should the driver stop?
choice_a: Only when a train is visibly approaching
choice_b: Only after the gate has completely lowered
choice_c: When the lights begin to flash and before the gate lowers across the road lane
choice_d: Drivers should proceed through gates as long as no train is in sight
explanation: At crossings with gates and flashing red lights and bells, the driver should stop when the lights begin to flash and before the gate lowers across the road lane, remaining stopped until the gates go up and the lights stop flashing.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 10 - School Buses, p. 10-8

question: When stopping at a railroad-highway crossing, how close to and how far from the nearest rail should the school bus stop, where the best view of the tracks is available?
choice_a: No closer than 25 feet and no farther than 75 feet from the nearest rail
choice_b: Exactly 10 feet from the nearest rail
choice_c: No closer than 15 feet and no farther than 50 feet from the nearest rail
choice_d: No closer than 5 feet and no farther than 20 feet from the nearest rail
explanation: At the crossing, the driver should stop no closer than 15 feet and no farther than 50 feet from the nearest rail, at the point offering the best view of the tracks.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 10 - School Buses, p. 10-8

question: If a school bus stalls or becomes trapped on railroad tracks, what should the driver do?
choice_a: Move everyone away from the tracks in the direction opposite the approaching train
choice_b: Attempt to move the bus off the tracks before evacuating anyone
choice_c: Get everyone out and off the tracks immediately, moving away from the tracks and toward the direction of the train
choice_d: Keep everyone on the bus and wait for the train to stop
explanation: If the bus stalls or is trapped on the tracks, the driver must get everyone out and off the tracks immediately, moving everyone far from the bus at an angle that is both away from the tracks and toward the train.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 10 - School Buses, p. 10-9

question: According to the manual, which vehicles are required by the Department of Transportation to have antilock braking systems (ABS)?
choice_a: Air brake vehicles built on or after March 1, 1998, and hydraulically braked trucks/buses with a GVWR of 10,000 lbs or more built on or after March 1, 1999
choice_b: Only buses built after March 1, 2005
choice_c: Only buses with a gross vehicle weight rating under 10,000 lbs
choice_d: All school buses, regardless of build date or brake type
explanation: The Department of Transportation requires ABS on air brake vehicles (trucks, buses, trailers, and converter dollies) built on or after March 1, 1998, and on hydraulically braked trucks and buses with a GVWR of 10,000 lbs or more built on or after March 1, 1999.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 10 - School Buses, p. 10-9

question: According to the manual, when should a school bus driver never back the bus?
choice_a: When the parking brake is set
choice_b: When backing at a student pick-up point after all students have boarded
choice_c: When a lookout has been posted
choice_d: When students are outside of the bus
explanation: Backing is strongly discouraged and the driver should never back a school bus when students are outside of the bus, since backing is dangerous and increases the risk of a collision.
source_note: AL CDL Manual (2005 CDL Testing System, Version: July 2017), Section 10 - School Buses, p. 10-10
